about: Build inputs: catalog/site.json and catalog/entries/; do not edit. Edit those files instead.

parts.title: Ranking under uncertainty
parts.lead: Estimates are noisy, so a league table of them is partly noise. A posterior says how sure we are of each unit and of each direction between two units.

parts.title: From ranks to grades
parts.lead: A grade report states the direction of every pair in different grades and stays silent on pairs in the same grade. Its risk adds the expected wrong directions and a price τ for each silent pair.

parts.title: Common rules
parts.lead: Tiers, flags and posterior cuts are grade reports too. Read as reports, they can be compared with the frontier at the same disclosure. Other questions, such as stability or filling a fixed number of places, need their own yardsticks.

parts.title: Multiple criteria
parts.lead: One common grade column can be assessed across criteria, or separate domain columns can retain a profile. Compare their report spaces, decisions and protection.

parts.title: Multidomain profiles
parts.lead: Separate ordered grades retain each domain in a profile. Additive risk can separate across domains, while joint protection can change which complete profile card is optimal.

parts.title: Cases
parts.lead: KRW's loss and its λ set against postrank's τ, then released case data read as postrank reports: firms in the KRW discrimination report card, California schools and Alabama counties.

parts.title: Tools
parts.lead: Your own posterior summaries in the browser, and a released case graded with your settings, with what the report states and leaves unsaid.

apps.name: case-zero
apps.title: A league table and a report card
apps.idea: The same 97 firms in a league table and in KRW's report card: the two reports say different things about pairs of firms.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-01 case-zero
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Introduction and section VI (Figure 7), and slides 4–5 and 61–63 (card layout); the gender card, section VIII (Figure 14). Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw).
apps.caption: Posterior means and central 90% intervals come from a smoothed version of KRW's posteriors (continuous cells with central intervals in place of KRW's posterior grids; the pr_case_krw data); KRW's Figure 7 caption says 95%.

shows: 1,219 run as the table does and 105 the other way
15 as the table does and 1 the other way
2 as the table does and 14 the other way
730 run as the table does and 1 the other way

apps.name: noisy-estimate
apps.title: One number, two parts
apps.idea: A reported estimate is its true value plus noise, and the noise changes each time the data are collected again.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-02 noisy-estimate
apps.credit: Built for this site; estimate-plus-noise model after Walters, Mixtape slides pp. 5–6; Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section III, Assumption 1 (stated before Section III.A), and talk slide 17; and the postrank theory book, ch. 2, “Teacher growth categories: evidence, precision, and the choice of assessment”.
apps.caption: Simulated estimates: each is the true value plus the SE times a random draw from the bell-shaped normal curve, and the seed fixes the draws.

apps.name: noisy-league
apps.title: Ranking noisy estimates
apps.idea: Ranking noisy estimates sends more of the noisiest units to the top and bottom places than their true values would, and replays show it is not one draw's luck.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-03 noisy-league
apps.credit: A simulated league built for this site; idea after the ebrecipe README and Walters (CCPR handout, p. 92; Mixtape slides, pp. 43–44).
apps.caption: A simulated league built for this site: thirty fictional units with fixed true values; each draw adds noise of the unit's SE to every true value, computed in this browser.

shows: the top 10 by estimate, 9 are in the true top 10
small units hold 4.35 of the 10 extreme positions
the truth, 3 small and 3 large units

apps.name: winners-curse
apps.title: Too good to be true at the top
apps.idea: Units that reach the top by their estimates have estimates above their true values on average; a posterior mean whose prior matches the true values' center and spread takes back about all of it.
apps.from: new angle · builds on v1 L-03's league; adds the top-k overshoot of estimates over true values, replay by replay, and its correction by the posterior mean
apps.credit: Built for this site; the upward bias of the top estimates after Walters (2024, Handbook of Labor Economics), section 3.5, and Andrews, Kitagawa and McCloskey (2024).
apps.caption: Each replay draws new estimates at the same true values and standard errors. The chosen prior gives the posterior means.

apps.name: shrinkage
apps.title: What a posterior adds
apps.idea: With one prior shared by all units, the posterior mean pulls imprecise estimates further toward the prior mean than precise ones, so it can reorder units, and only units whose precisions differ.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-04 shrinkage (both views)
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), sections III, V.B and V.E and slide 49; the postrank theory book, ch. 20; and Walters, Mixtape slides p. 27.
apps.caption: The posterior is calculated from the chosen normal prior and the estimates with their standard errors.

apps.name: shrinkage-price
apps.title: How much to shrink
apps.idea: The prior SD is set or estimated by the producer: over many draws the distance to the true values is smallest near the true spread (prior centered on their average), and the pair probabilities postrank reads move with it.
apps.from: new angle · builds on v1 L-04 view 2; adds curves over the whole prior-SD range: the distance to the true values (with its closed-form expectation) and what postrank reads from the posterior, its pair probabilities (how many directions are near certain); the report and the share it claims are 2.9's
apps.credit: Built for this site; normal-normal shrinkage after Walters, Mixtape slides p. 27; a producer's hyperparameters and a fixed-parameter experiment, after the postrank theory book, ch. 18.
apps.caption: The posterior is calculated from the chosen normal prior and the estimates with their standard errors.

apps.name: posterior-pipeline
apps.title: Where the posterior comes from
apps.idea: Of data, model, posterior and decision, postrank does only the last step: it reads a posterior and makes grades.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-05 posterior-pipeline, plus a working two-unit chain (estimate and SE, prior, posterior, π, decision at τ)
apps.credit: After Walters, Mixtape slides p. 13, and Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section III.A–B and slides 43–52.
apps.caption: Each box names its source in the theory book or the package documentation. The box headers show no computed numbers; the two units in the stages under them are computed in this browser.

apps.name: two-units
apps.title: Two units, one probability
apps.idea: One number, π = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y), says how sure we are of a direction between two units.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-07 two-units (core views)
apps.credit: π for two independent normal posteriors; the case with both SDs equal to 1 is Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.E, Example 1, and slide 27.
apps.caption: A specified joint distribution for two independent normal posterior values.

presets.label: Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .60 (B much less precise)
Means 1.20 and .95, SDs .20 and .20 (tutorial sites A and B)

apps.name: correlated-units
apps.title: When two posteriors move together
apps.idea: When two jointly normal posteriors are correlated, the SD of their difference changes and π moves away from or toward one half, but never crosses it.
apps.from: new angle · v1 L-07 Deeper box 1 (correlation) as the main view; adds the joint-posterior ellipse with the region θ_A > θ_B shaded, and a preset with the positive correlation a shared, uncertain prior mean induces
apps.credit: Built for this site (bivariate normal; a shared, uncertain prior mean makes posteriors move together); dependence after the postrank theory book, ch. 9 and 18.
apps.caption: Two posterior values whose dependence can change.

apps.name: beyond-normal
apps.title: Same means, different directions
apps.idea: Two posteriors with the same margins can give opposite directions (1/3 against 2/3), and a two-bump posterior can have the larger mean but the smaller chance of being higher.
apps.from: new angle · v1 L-07 Deeper boxes 2 and 3 (joint laws Q1 and Q2; the mixture); adds an editable 3 x 3 joint law
apps.credit: Joint laws after the postrank theory book, ch. 9 (Fig. f09b).
apps.caption: The examples specify posterior distributions with fixed marginal means.

apps.name: interval-overlap
apps.title: Intervals do not decide directions
apps.idea: Two posterior intervals can overlap while one direction is very likely.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 L-06 interval-overlap, touch view
apps.credit: Two posteriors set by hand for this site; interval reading after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section IV.C and Figure 3.
apps.caption: Two independent normal posteriors with equal standard deviations.

apps.name: overlap-in-the-league
apps.title: 435 pairs: overlap against direction
apps.idea: Sorting the league's 435 pairs by interval overlap and by direction probability shows that overlapping intervals often hide a likely direction.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 L-06 interval-overlap, league view
apps.credit: Built for this site; interval reading after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section IV.C.
apps.caption: A normal posterior gives the marginal intervals and pairwise probabilities for the simulated league.

apps.name: pairwise-matrix
apps.title: All pairs at once
apps.idea: With every pair's π in one matrix ordered by posterior mean, the uncertain pairs gather near the diagonal (for independent normal posteriors).
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-08 pairwise-matrix
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Figure 2A and slide 38 (first names) and slide 54 (firms).
apps.caption: The examples use specified posterior distributions for the fictional units.

apps.name: which-ranking
apps.title: Three rankings from one posterior
apps.idea: One posterior can rank units differently by posterior mean, by expected rank and by the chance of being on top when the posteriors differ in width or shape, and each unit's own rank is uncertain.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-09 which-ranking; adds a scale switch (θ or √θ on the ch. 19 law, θ or exp(kθ) on the league) under which only the posterior-mean ranking moves
apps.credit: Built for this site; the three-unit law after the postrank theory book, ch. 19; expected ranks after ch. 5; the scale switch after ch. 4 and 12; rankings by posterior means after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section IV.B and the notes to Figure 2C, and talk slide 59.
apps.caption: The three-unit law after the postrank theory book, ch. 19, and a simulated league built for this site; every summary is computed in this browser.

shows: Two units are never in the top ten

apps.name: majority-wins
apps.title: Majority wins and expected rank
apps.idea: For independent normal posteriors, counting the pairs each unit more likely wins gives the posterior-mean order; on KRW's race gaps it gives an order of its own, which KRW's λ = 1 race card follows.
apps.from: new angle · v1 L-09 Deeper box (the law on orders); adds majority-win counts, on the league (where they equal the posterior-mean order) and on KRW's 97 firms (where they differ), and KRW's λ = 1 cards (the gender card's one tie is within KRW's solver tolerance)
apps.credit: Law on orders after the postrank theory book, ch. 10; shared grades at λ = 1 after ch. 16; Condorcet ranks after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.F, whose remark that the count of wins equals the posterior mean of the rank (the expected rank) does not hold in general (postrank theory book, ch. 10). Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). Cards computed with KRW's code (KRW replication companion) under KRW's archived pair probabilities.
apps.caption: The law on orders after the postrank theory book, ch. 10, a simulated league built for this site and KRW's 97 firms; every order and count is computed in this browser from each data set's pair probabilities.

apps.name: ranking-claims
apps.title: A ranking makes many claims
apps.idea: A strict ranking of n units makes n(n − 1)/2 claims, and the posterior expects many of them to be wrong.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 L-10 ranking-claims (with both More boxes as panels)
apps.credit: Firms from Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), ranked here by posterior mean; the school count from the California Department of Education, 2026 California School Dashboard chronic absenteeism data, academic year 2025–26, via postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde); six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial.
apps.caption: Counts and expected counts are computed in this browser from each data set's pair probabilities: the six sites of the postrank tutorial, a simulated league whose posterior is set by hand, and KRW's 97 firms.

apps.name: mc-error
apps.title: Probabilities from draws carry noise
apps.idea: An error probability estimated from posterior draws has Monte Carlo error; pairs near τ can flip between runs, but the report need not change with them.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-09; postrank vignette m6 (pairwise MCSE and Monte Carlo fragility); picture: estimated against exact error probabilities with ±2 MCSE as the number of draws S changes, the simultaneous envelope (the package's form, the book's noted), the pairs flagged fragile, and the report chosen from the estimates beside the one from the exact values
apps.credit: After the postrank vignette m6, “Monte Carlo uncertainty and diagnostics”, and the postrank theory book, ch. 15.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial; their normal law is set by hand, and the draws are simulated in this browser.

apps.name: chain-draws
apps.title: Draws that remember
apps.idea: Successive MCMC draws are usually positively correlated, so a pair probability estimated from them carries more Monte Carlo error than the iid formula says, and an iid error bound can fail far more often than its α.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 15 (dependent Monte Carlo; the two-state chain); postrank vignette m6 (loss traces, MCMC diagnostics) and pr_toy_mcmc; picture: a two-state trace with its running estimate and, under it, the spread of the estimate over many chains against the iid reference, the iid ±2 MCSE band and radius; the reader sets the stay probability, S and the number of chains
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 15, and the postrank vignette m6.
apps.caption: The two directions have probability one half each, as in chapter 15 of the postrank theory book. The chains start from that distribution.

apps.name: one-pair
apps.title: One pair: state or withhold
apps.idea: For a pair on its own, state a direction only when its chance of being wrong is below the withholding cost τ.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 G-01 one-pair
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 10 (Fig. f10a), and Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 18–20.
apps.caption: One pair on its own: a wrong stated direction costs 1, silence costs τ, and the two true values are never equal.

shows: all three actions are equally good

apps.name: report-builder
apps.title: A report is many pair decisions
apps.idea: Moving units between grade boxes states every pair across grades and withholds every pair inside a grade.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 G-02 report-builder
apps.credit: Block reading after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slide 56.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial, score A: a higher score means a higher priority. A report here is only a grade vector; no probability enters here.

presets.label: A, then B to E, then F

apps.name: how-many-reports
apps.title: How many grade reports are there?
apps.idea: Grade reports far outnumber strict rankings (13 for three units, 4,683 for six, 545,835 for eight), while a cap or a fixed order leaves far fewer (for eight units, 6,051 with at most three grades, 128 along one order).
apps.from: new angle · builds on v1 G-02 and G-08; adds the count of reports by n and family (ordered set partitions)
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 14, and the postrank vignette m5.
apps.caption: Exact counts of ordered grade reports from the postrank engine; counts only, with no posterior or optimization.

apps.name: price-of-silence
apps.title: The price of silence
apps.idea: With a price τ on silence, risk is E/M + τ(M − N)/M, and the best report moves with τ; your own report can be scored beside it.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 G-03 price-of-silence (with the your-report bar)
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 23–25, re-expressed as postrank risk.
apps.caption: We use the normal posteriors for score A at six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial. The calculation evaluates every eligible report.

apps.name: tau-path
apps.title: The best report along τ
apps.idea: Each report's risk is a straight line in τ; where the lower envelope bends, the best report changes.
apps.from: new angle · builds on v1 G-03; adds the risk lines of all reports in τ and the breakpoints of the envelope
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 11 and 16.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial, reading score only; normal posteriors set by hand for teaching. Every report in the selected family is evaluated in this browser.

apps.name: coherence
apps.title: Why a report must be coherent
apps.idea: Choices made pair by pair can be impossible to print as a grade report, and the best printable report then costs more.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 G-04 coherence, the pairwise-choice view
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Example 1 and slide 27; coherence after the postrank theory book, ch. 10.
apps.caption: Independent normal posteriors in KRW’s Example 1. A/B/C name their first/second/third firms; their middle mean is ω₂.

apps.name: coherence-finite
apps.title: Thirteen reports for three units
apps.idea: Under one finite three-unit law, for τ between 1/10 and 1/4 no report prints the pairwise choices; all 13 reports show what the best printable one costs (11/60 against 1/6 at τ = 1/5).
apps.from: v1 view · v1 G-04 coherence, the finite-law view
apps.credit: Three-unit law after the postrank theory book, ch. 10.
apps.caption: Three-unit finite law from the postrank theory book, chapter 10; all thirteen reports evaluated in the browser.

apps.name: disclosed-errors
apps.title: How often are stated directions wrong?
apps.idea: E/N is the share of stated directions expected to be wrong, and for the exact best report of a family that can withhold every pair it is at most τ; draws of the true values make it concrete. The chance that every stated direction is right depends on the joint law, beyond these pairwise errors.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 G-05 disclosed-errors
apps.credit: Definitions after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 22 and 25–26; finite law after the postrank theory book, chapter 10. Joint-event interpretation after the postrank theory book, chapter 6.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites with independent normal latent values and a three-unit finite law; posteriors taken as given, not fitted by postrank.

apps.name: reported-and-realized
apps.title: Reported and realized error
apps.idea: For a fixed report, its claimed wrong share and its expectation under an explicit reference law differ by at most the largest pair-error probability gap; a single fixed-truth realization can lie on either side.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 18 (reported and realized loss; a producer's model); builds on v1 G-05; a prior-SD control (from 1.6) sets the claim against realized shares at fixed true values, which is not the calibration identity of ch. 18; picture: a fixed report's claimed E/N under an assumed prior SD (the reader's control) beside its expected share under another law and the realized shares over replays of the simulated league
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 18.
apps.caption: Simulated league of 30 units with deterministic true values and SEs .20, .10 and .05. Independent normal-normal teaching laws with prior mean 0; the reference prior SD is .15. Fixed-truth observation replays are not the conditional calibration identity.

apps.name: frontier
apps.title: The frontier
apps.idea: Every report as a point (N, E): the lower hull is the frontier, and τ is the slope of a line that touches it.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 G-06 frontier, the hull view
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 58–60; frontier after the postrank theory book, ch. 16.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial, score A only; their normal posteriors are specified for teaching and taken as given. Every report of the family is evaluated in this browser.

apps.name: frontier-mixtures
apps.title: Mixtures between frontier corners
apps.idea: Between two vertices the frontier is a mixture of two complete reports (on the six sites no report lies there); with all reports and no latent ties it ends at a strict ranking, on a line of slope 1/2.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 G-06 frontier, the mixture view
apps.credit: Four-unit law after the postrank theory book, ch. 16.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites and stipulated finite laws; complete reports are randomized at a specified mean disclosure.

apps.name: families
apps.title: Families of reports
apps.idea: An optimum is always the best within a stated family of reports: all reports, at most G grades, exactly G grades, or cuts of one order.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 G-08 families
apps.credit: Built on postrank's families (Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 21, 24 and 57, use no cap); four-unit example after the postrank theory book, ch. 14.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial, or the theory book's four-unit two-criterion law; the declared family determines the search.

apps.name: report-card
apps.title: Reading a report card
apps.idea: A report card shows the grades, each unit's posterior interval and the expected share of directions between two grades that are wrong.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 G-07 report-card
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 61–63 and 69; card layout after the postrank package's report-card plot.
apps.caption: The grade report uses the posterior specified for the example.

shows: With one grade shown there is nothing to compare yet.

apps.name: two-denominators
apps.title: Wrong among stated, wrong among all
apps.idea: KRW's DR divides expected wrong directions by all pairs and E/N by the stated pairs, so a card that states few pairs can show a small DR beside a large E/N: DR = (N/M) × E/N.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 G-09 krw-bridge, denominators view
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 22 and 25–26. Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw).
apps.caption: The six-site posterior is given for teaching; the race card retains archived statistics and is evaluated on released probabilities.

apps.name: ties-and-withholding
apps.title: When true values can be equal
apps.idea: When true values can be exactly equal, a shared grade still claims no equality, and postrank's equality-neutral risk prices stated and withheld pairs differently from the weak loss.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-10; postrank vignette m4 (the m4 tie law, equality-neutral risk); picture: the three action risks for a pair whose true values can be equal, under the weak loss and the equality-neutral risk, with the all-withheld baseline R₀ beside τ and the switch points (vignette m4's law)
apps.credit: After the postrank vignette m4.
apps.caption: Complete synthetic law after postrank vignette m4; weak-error and equality-neutral loss are different decision conventions.

apps.name: computing-grades
apps.title: How the best report is found
apps.idea: This browser searches small families report by report, dynamic programming cuts one declared order exactly, and postrank's solver takes the joint problem and reports its status, bound and gap.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-08; theory book ch. 14; postrank vignette m5 (enumeration, fixed-order DP, MIP with status, bound and gap); picture: family sizes on a log axis, the 0/1 patterns of three units, the dynamic-programming table filling cell by cell, and a HiGHS solve with its incumbent risk, bound, gap and status
apps.credit: After the postrank vignette m5 and the theory book, ch. 14.
apps.caption: Family counts and search results computed in this browser. Six fictional sites use the postrank tutorial score-A posterior; the joint solver uses a frozen simulated league. Optimization answers only for its stated family and supplied probabilities.

apps.name: another-law
apps.title: Judging a report under another law
apps.idea: A report chosen under one posterior and judged under another can have a different risk; within the same family its regret is at most twice the largest weighted gap between the two laws' pair error probabilities, plus the optimizer's gap.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-11; theory book ch. 16 and 18 (regret under a different law); picture: two posteriors for the same units, a report chosen under one and judged under both, its regret and the bound 2d + η
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 16 and 18.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites, reading score only: two independent normal laws set by hand for teaching. A law is declared for selection and another for evaluation; this comparison does not establish empirical calibration.

apps.name: chosen-and-judged
apps.title: Scored on the draws that chose it
apps.idea: A report chosen on posterior draws can look better or worse on them than under the exact law, though better on average; the gap is at most N/M times the draws' largest pair-probability error, which shrinks as draws grow.
apps.from: new concept · postrank vignette m6 (fixed and selected actions; cross-fitting as the package view of fold grades) and theory book ch. 15 (the envelope covers selection on the same draws); picture: reruns of S draws, each run's chosen report scored on its own draws against its exact risk, the signed gap over runs, and the regret bound 2δ_w + η
apps.credit: After the postrank vignette m6 and the theory book, ch. 15.
apps.caption: Six fictional normal posteriors; reports selected from independent posterior draws and evaluated on those same draws and the exact declared law. A separate cached package toy shows fold reports.

apps.name: averaging-errors
apps.title: Three ways to average a wrong share
apps.idea: Over datasets, or outcomes of a randomized report, the wrong share of stated directions has three averages that generally differ: a ratio of expected counts, a mean over datasets that state something, and a mean counting silent ones as zero.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 8 and 16 (disclosed-error estimands) and App. B; v1 storyboard P-11, the error view; picture: three dataset cards with editable (wrong, stated) counts and the three averages as bars beside Pr(N > 0) and the mean disclosure; modes for a randomized report and for replicated leagues
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 8 and 16.
apps.caption: Three-outcome evaluation, a lottery over fixed reports, and simulated repeated datasets; the three averaging conventions answer different questions.

apps.name: one-correction
apps.title: One correction moves other grades
apps.idea: Grades are chosen together, so correcting one unit's input, or dropping a unit, can change the relation between two other units.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 17 (information sets) and ch. 21 (transparency, appeal, documentation); postrank_compare() relations; picture: the card before and after the reader corrects one unit's mean or SD, or drops a unit, with the relation-change matrix and the count of changed pairs between units the reader did not touch
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 17 and 21.
apps.caption: Independent normal teaching posteriors. Six-site reports are optimized in their named full or capped family; the frozen league uses best cuts of a recomputed expected-rank order. Removed units are excluded, not graded last.

apps.name: fixed-tiers
apps.title: Fixed tiers
apps.idea: A quantile-tier rule is a grade report chosen without the posterior, and the posterior still says how many of its stated directions to expect wrong.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 R-01 fixed-tiers
apps.credit: Simulated data; rule definition after the postrank theory book, ch. 17.
apps.caption: Thirty simulated units, cut into tiers by their estimates; the chance a direction is wrong comes from a normal posterior (prior mean 0, SD .15).

apps.name: tier-sizes
apps.title: Tier sizes fix disclosure
apps.idea: Tier sizes alone set how many pairs a rule states, whatever the estimates (when no two are equal); for a given number of tiers, balanced sizes state the most.
apps.from: new angle · v1 R-01's formula panel and its 1/1/28 counterexample; adds editable tier sizes, the N of every size pattern at one G and the closed form when G divides n
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 9, 16 and 17.
apps.caption: Ordered positive tier-size patterns, each with equal weight; no posterior errors are inferred from disclosure counts. Quantile ties are kept together by the package.

apps.name: evidence-flags
apps.title: Flags from standardized evidence
apps.idea: A flag rule on standardized evidence is a report with at most three grades (flagged above, not flagged, flagged below), and precision moves units across the flags.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 R-02 evidence-flags, the two-unit view
apps.credit: Two-unit example after the postrank theory book, ch. 2.
apps.caption: Two units against the reference 0; independent normal posteriors price the stated direction.

apps.name: flags-in-the-league
apps.title: Flags in a league
apps.idea: In a league, a flag rule can state directions that run against the order of the estimates.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 R-02 evidence-flags, the league view
apps.credit: Built for this site; flag rule after the postrank theory book, ch. 2 and 17.
apps.caption: Thirty simulated units; the mean of their estimates is treated as a fixed reference; independent normal posteriors price the flag report.

apps.name: posterior-tiers
apps.title: Tiers from posterior summaries
apps.idea: At one τ and cap, the risk never rises from posterior-mean tiers to the best cuts of their order to the best report of all, as each family holds the one before; on the eight units the last two coincide.
apps.from: v1 whole · v1 R-03 posterior-tiers
apps.credit: League built for this site (the eight units are its U01–U08); 30-site example from the postrank package (synthetic); tiers after the postrank theory book, ch. 17.
apps.caption: One supplied posterior and one withholding price for every rule; fixed tiers, optimized cuts within named orders, and exhaustive optimization only on the eight units.

apps.name: order-misses
apps.title: When the order misses the best report
apps.idea: On a three-unit law, for τ above .15 the best cuts of the posterior-mean order miss the best report of all, which a cut of the expected-rank order attains; one example, not a general failing of posterior means.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 R-03 posterior-tiers, the chapter 19 example (and v2's posterior-tiers)
apps.credit: Three-unit example after the postrank theory book, ch. 19.
apps.caption: Three units with two possible states of their true values; exact probabilities, every report evaluated in this browser.

apps.name: rule-comparison
apps.title: Compare rules at the same disclosure
apps.idea: A rule is compared with the frontier at its own disclosure, the lowest expected wrong count a report or a mixture of two in the family attains with as many stated pairs, not with the best report at some τ.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 R-04 rule-comparison, the same-disclosure view
apps.credit: Frontier after the postrank theory book, ch. 16; rules as points after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), slides 58–60.
apps.caption: Units U01–U08 of the simulated league under a normal posterior (prior mean 0, SD .15); flags against the mean of all 30 league estimates.

apps.name: same-tau-or-same-n
apps.title: Same price or same disclosure?
apps.idea: At one τ a rule's risk also charges it for the pairs it leaves unsaid; at its own N only its expected wrong directions are set against the frontier.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 R-04 rule-comparison, the same-τ view
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 16–17.
apps.caption: Units U01–U08, or all thirty units, of the simulated league under a normal posterior (prior mean 0, SD .15); flags against the mean of all 30 league estimates.

apps.name: deciles-quartiles
apps.title: Deciles and quartiles of posterior means
apps.idea: Deciles and quartiles of KRW's posterior means sit inside the curve traced by KRW's cards along λ: for each, some card has a lower discordance rate and a higher informativeness.
apps.from: new angle · builds on 3.5 and 5.5; adds deciles and quartiles of KRW's posterior means on KRW's two axes (KRW sections IV.B and V.E, Figures 2C and 6), evaluated with postrank's pair probabilities
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section IV.B (Figure 2C) and section V.E (Figure 6). Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). Cards computed with KRW's code (KRW replication companion) under KRW's archived pair probabilities.
apps.caption: Posterior-mean tiers and archived KRW cards evaluated under the same released signed-target pair probabilities.

apps.name: naive-thresholding
apps.title: Pairwise thresholds no report can print
apps.idea: Thresholding each pair on its own leaves triples of firms that no grade report can print; the card's grade blocks repair them by withholding some confident pairs and stating some doubtful ones.
apps.from: new angle · v1 S-02 heat map, second stage (pairs past the threshold), and KRW section V.E (naive thresholding); adds the unprintable triples among the 97 firms (including two pairs left unsaid with the third stated; the race baseline has no strict 3-cycles, while the signed gender target has one at λ=1), their change with λ and their overlap with the card's blocks
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section V.E, and the postrank theory book, ch. 10. Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). Cards computed with KRW's code (KRW replication companion) under KRW's archived pair probabilities.
apps.caption: Strict isolated pair thresholds on the released KRW law, compared with the current archived card; shared grades make no equality claim.

apps.name: better-on-average
apps.title: Better on average, not in every draw
apps.idea: The best report has the smallest expected loss within its family under the law that chose it; in a single draw, a common rule can do better.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 16 (conditional Bayes dominance) and ch. 18; postrank vignette m2; picture: the per-draw realized loss of the best report against a common rule's, with the 45° line, the share of draws the rule wins and the mean difference; a toggle takes the rule outside the family
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 16.
apps.caption: Conditional posterior experiment: both reports are selected once from the declared law and then fixed across paired whole-state draws. Dominance concerns expected total reporting loss within the named family.

apps.name: stability
apps.title: Measure again, grade again
apps.idea: Measuring again and grading again changes some pair relations; stability has to be read beside disclosure, because withholding every pair is perfectly stable.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 17 (stability needs its own repeated-data law); picture: two replications of the league side by side with their relation changes, and a replay histogram of the share of changed relations beside N/M and E/N for several rules
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 17.
apps.caption: Fixed-truth paired measurement experiment; every observation refits its stipulated posterior.

apps.name: one-place
apps.title: A grade is not an allocation
apps.idea: With a fixed number of places or a fixed threshold, posterior means, the chances of being in the top or above the threshold, and the grades can pick differently; using grades for either needs one more rule.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 17 (selection benchmarks; threshold classification with asymmetric costs), ch. 19 and ch. 21; picture: rules as points of expected selected value against expected overlap with the true top (in threshold mode, against expected classification loss), each with its reporting risk; the reader sets the places or the threshold, τ and the law
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 17 and 19.
apps.caption: Supplied tie-free conditional laws; native expected value, top-set overlap and asymmetric threshold costs are evaluated separately from reporting loss.

apps.name: several-criteria
apps.title: Units measured on several criteria
apps.idea: Units can be ordered differently on different criteria, and each criterion has its own pair probabilities.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-01; postrank vignette m2; picture: the thirty sites on three criteria and the six sites on two scores, with each criterion's posterior intervals, its own order and the pairs whose criteria point opposite ways
apps.credit: After the postrank vignette m2 and the theory book, ch. 12.
apps.caption: Synthetic postrank Normal laws: thirty sites on three criteria or six sites on two scores. Marginal posterior intervals and mean orders, not optimized grades.

apps.name: conflict-pairs
apps.title: Where criteria disagree
apps.idea: When criteria disagree about a pair's direction, stating either direction costs something even with no uncertainty, when both sides carry positive weight; on a posterior, uncertainty and conflict mix.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 12 (conflicting pairs); picture: a map of the pairs on which the criteria disagree, with each such pair's three costs at equal weights (either direction, withholding) and the smaller weighted error
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 12.
apps.caption: Synthetic supplied laws after the postrank theory book, ch. 12 and 19. Isolated-pair costs, not an optimized common grade.

apps.name: two-scores
apps.title: One grade for two scores
apps.idea: One grade report for two scores: the weight decides how much each score's wrong directions count, and so which conflicting pairs are stated.
apps.from: v2 refill · v2 two-scores rebuilt from v1 storyboard P-02
apps.credit: On the postrank package's six fictional sites (scores A and B).
apps.caption: Six fictional sites; independent Normal posteriors set by hand for teaching; postrank does not fit them.

apps.name: weight-path
apps.title: The best report along the weight
apps.idea: Moving the weight changes the best report a few times, and each score's error share moves in steps.
apps.from: new angle · the step figure v2 two-scores left out; adds the reports on each weight interval
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 11.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites; exact weight intervals in the displayed report family. Risks at different weights use different losses.

apps.name: common-grade-cost
apps.title: What each criterion gives up
apps.idea: Under a common report, each criterion's risk is at least as high as under its own best report in the same family; the difference is Δ_k.
apps.from: v2 refill · v2 common-grade-cost rebuilt from v1 storyboard P-03
apps.credit: The cost of a common grade is a postrank package concept (vignette m2).
apps.caption: Six fictional sites with live error weights, or fixed archived thirty-site analyses from postrank.

apps.name: composite-or-criterion
apps.title: Composite or criterion directions?
apps.idea: Getting the direction of a weighted composite right and getting each criterion's directions right are different goals and can pick different reports.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-04; theory book ch. 12; postrank vignette m2 (estimand costs); picture: the costs of A above B, B above A and withholding under the criterion-direction loss and the composite-direction loss, the action each prefers, and a transform control under which grades stay and composites move
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 12 (four-unit law after ch. 19), and the postrank vignette m2.
apps.caption: Supplied synthetic laws after the postrank theory book, ch. 12 and19, and vignette m2. Both losses use one law, withholding price and report family.

apps.name: error-budgets
apps.title: A budget for each criterion
apps.idea: A budget on each criterion's expected error share removes reports, so the best remaining report has a weighted risk at least as high.
apps.from: v2 refill · v2 error-budgets rebuilt from v1 storyboard P-05
apps.credit: Protections after the postrank theory book, ch. 13.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites with independent normal posteriors for scores A and B.

apps.name: criterion-mixture
apps.title: Weights as a randomly chosen criterion
apps.idea: Choosing one auxiliary criterion for an entire fixed report reproduces its weighted risk. Opposing criteria can make both strict directions costly, while a coherent report can still state either.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-06; theory book ch. 11 (the mixture reading) and ch. 12 (when stating an isolated conflicting pair costs at least τ); picture: the weighted risk computed both ways, the three costs of the conflicting pair against τ, and, at τ .35 with no cap, the six-site optimum 1/2/2/3/4/5, which states two such pairs
apps.credit: Mixture reading after the postrank theory book, ch. 11.
apps.caption: Synthetic supplied laws after the postrank theory book, ch. 11–12. One auxiliary criterion selects an entire unit vector after the report is fixed.

apps.name: worst-criterion
apps.title: Guarding the worse criterion
apps.idea: Instead of the weighted best, one can choose the report that makes the worse criterion's risk smallest.
apps.from: v2 refill · v2 worst-criterion rebuilt from v1 storyboard P-07
apps.credit: Mixture reading after the postrank theory book, ch. 11; minimax after ch. 13.
apps.caption: Expected-criterion minimax and weighted risk in the same displayed report family.

apps.name: choosing-settings
apps.title: Choosing τ, the cap and the weights
apps.idea: Within one fixed family a larger τ never lowers the exact best report's disclosure. Changing τ or weights changes the loss; changing the cap changes the feasible family. The grid separates these effects.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard P-12; postrank_settings_grid() and postrank_sensitivity(); picture: a step chart of N against τ with the grades on each interval and E_k/N lines (risks marked not comparable across τ), and a grid over τ, the cap and the weights
apps.credit: After the postrank vignette a7 (figures and sensitivity).
apps.caption: Exact six-site settings or fixed public archived sensitivity analyses.

apps.name: draws-to-errors
apps.title: From draws to pair errors
apps.idea: Each posterior draw is one joint state of every unit on every criterion; counting orders within each criterion gives the pair errors the weighted risk needs, and shuffling one unit's draws keeps its margins but changes them.
apps.from: new concept · postrank vignette m3 (posterior inputs; the package toy's 32 draws); picture: the draws as whole states, each criterion's order counted draw by draw into running shares, and a shuffle toggle that keeps one unit's margins but changes the error probabilities
apps.credit: After the postrank vignettes m3 and inputs-and-producers.
apps.caption: The package toy’s actual 32 complete IID states. Synthetic: no real units, observations or fitted models. Data license CC BY 4.0.

apps.name: why-withheld
apps.title: Why do these two share a grade?
apps.idea: A shared grade can come from an uncertain direction, from criteria that conflict, from coherence with other pairs or from the family's limits, and the grade does not say which.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 10, 12, 19 and 21; postrank vignette a2 (pairwise support); picture: the relation matrix; clicking a shared-grade pair opens four tests (the isolated rule, the criteria's directions, stated alone, the family) and the cheapest report that states the pair, with its extra risk
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 19 and 21. Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). 12-school teaching subset as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde).
apps.caption: Six fictional sites and restated finite teaching laws; case views carry their released conditioning, attribution and license notices. Four nonexclusive tests under the supplied law; same grade means not compared.

apps.name: pairs-leave-open
apps.title: What pair probabilities leave open
apps.idea: Pair probabilities fix the weighted risk but not the chance that a composite direction is right or that every stated direction is right; those need the joint law.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 11 and 19; postrank vignettes m2 and m3 (information requirements) and inputs-and-producers; picture: a joint-law editor for two units on two criteria (presets together and opposite), where what the pair probabilities fix stays locked while composite and joint quantities move
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 11 (four-unit law after ch. 19), and the postrank vignette m3.
apps.caption: Restated synthetic finite laws after the postrank theory book, chapters 11 and 19, and vignettes m2/m3. Within-criterion pair errors determine additive expected risk; composite and joint-event probabilities use the complete stipulated law.

apps.name: estimated-budgets
apps.title: A budget met on estimated probabilities
apps.idea: With pair probabilities estimated from draws, a report can meet an error budget on the estimates yet fail it under the exact law; when the draws' error bound holds, inner and outer families bracket the compliant reports.
apps.from: new concept · theory book ch. 15 (estimated protections; the bound holds with probability at least 1 − α); postrank vignette m6; postrank_protection_envelopes(); picture: a membership grid of reports against inner, estimated, exact and outer families, and a number line per report with the estimated and exact E/N, q and q ± ε; the reader sets t, ε and the exact-count switch
apps.credit: After the postrank theory book, ch. 15.
apps.caption: After the postrank theory book, ch. 15; supplied-law expected-error protections, with signed inner and outer thresholds.

apps.name: profile-common-vs-domain
apps.title: Common or profile?
apps.idea: Common grades or separate priorities.
apps.from: P2 multidomain profile theory
apps.credit: JoonHo Lee; postrank multidomain profile decisions (postrank 1.2.0).
apps.caption: Complete finite teaching law; exact arithmetic; optimum within the stated candidate bank.

apps.name: profile-separability
apps.title: Separate or joint?
apps.idea: Additive loss. A joint guard can change the choices.
apps.from: P2 multidomain profile theory
apps.credit: JoonHo Lee; postrank multidomain profile decisions (postrank 1.2.0).
apps.caption: Complete finite teaching law; exact arithmetic; optimum within the stated candidate bank.

presets.label: Independent domains with a joint guard

apps.name: profile-dependence
apps.title: Error overlap
apps.idea: Same domain laws. Different decisions.
apps.from: P2 multidomain profile theory
apps.credit: JoonHo Lee; postrank multidomain profile decisions (postrank 1.2.0).
apps.caption: Complete finite teaching law; exact arithmetic; optimum within the stated candidate bank.

apps.name: profile-resolution
apps.title: Budget and grades
apps.idea: More budget can shift detail between domains.
apps.from: P2 multidomain profile theory
apps.credit: JoonHo Lee; postrank multidomain profile decisions (postrank 1.2.0).
apps.caption: Complete finite teaching law; exact arithmetic; optimum within the stated candidate bank.

apps.name: fictional-site-profiles
apps.title: Site profiles
apps.idea: Forty sites. Two priorities. Saved fictional reports.
apps.from: P2 multidomain profile theory
apps.credit: JoonHo Lee; postrank multidomain profile decisions (postrank 1.2.0).
apps.caption: Saved fictional forty-site cards from postrank 1.2.0; display only, with no runtime reoptimization or intended-posterior certificate.

apps.name: lambda-tau
apps.title: KRW's λ and postrank's τ
apps.idea: KRW's reward λ for a correct direction and postrank's withholding cost τ = λ/(1 + λ) pick the same reports under the same posterior and the same family, when true values cannot be equal.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 G-09 krw-bridge, the λ-τ view
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II and slides 18–21, 24–26 and 29–30; correspondence after the postrank theory book, ch. 10.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites with a specified posterior.

apps.name: krw-axes
apps.title: Two ways to score a report
apps.idea: Scoring the 4,683 reports of six sites by KRW's loss at λ and by postrank's risk at τ = λ/(1 + λ) orders them the same way: one is an increasing linear function of the other.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 G-09 krw-bridge, the two-axes view
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section II and slides 24–26 and 29–30.
apps.caption: Six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial, score A only; their independent normal posteriors are specified for teaching and taken as given. Every one of the 4,683 reports is evaluated under both objectives. The separate 97-firm grid card was computed under KRW’s archived probabilities and is evaluated as a fixed report.

apps.name: krw-card
apps.title: KRW's race and gender cards
apps.idea: On KRW's cards for 97 firms, grade 1 is the end the posterior places highest, yet coherence also states doubtful directions; three on the gender card, whose end grades hold gaps of opposite sign, are more likely wrong than right.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 S-02 case-krw-race, the card view with its header boxes; adds a criterion switch (race or gender, shared with 5.4 and 5.5)
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section VI (Figure 7), section VIII (Figure 14) and slides 53–63 and 72–80. Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw).
apps.caption: All 97 firms; exact released contact-gap pair probabilities and supplied central 90% intervals. The data describe KRW’s historical experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.

apps.name: krw-heatmap
apps.title: Which firm pairs the card states
apps.idea: Laying the card's blocks over the 4,656 pair probabilities shows the pairs it states and the confident pairs it leaves unsaid.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 S-02 case-krw-race, the heat-map view
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section V.E (Figure 5A) and slides 54–56. Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). Cards computed with KRW's code (KRW replication companion) under KRW's archived pair probabilities.
apps.caption: All 97 firms; exact released contact-gap pair probabilities and supplied central 90% intervals. The data describe KRW’s historical experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.

apps.name: krw-lambda
apps.title: KRW's cards along λ
apps.idea: Along KRW's λ grid, cards with larger λ tend to state more pairs, with a larger share of them expected wrong.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 S-02 case-krw-race, the λ-grid view (and v2's krw-race)
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section V.E (Figures 5A and 6), section VI (Figure 7), section VI.B (Figure 10A), and slides 53–63. Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw).
apps.caption: All 97 firms; exact released contact-gap pair probabilities and supplied central 90% intervals. The data describe KRW’s historical experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.

apps.name: signed-or-absolute
apps.title: Signed or absolute gender gap
apps.idea: Grading the signed gender gap and grading its size answer different questions: which firm has the larger gap in size does not follow from the signed pair probabilities.
apps.from: new angle · builds on 5.3's gender card; adds the absolute (folded) gender target of pr_case_krw with its own pair probabilities, and two reports computed the same way (the best cuts of each target's expected-rank order, at most 4 grades at τ .20, labeled optimal within this order) with the pairs whose order differs
apps.credit: Signed and absolute targets after the postrank theory book, ch. 4 and 20, and the postrank vignette a3; gender gaps after Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section VIII (gender target). Firms as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw).
apps.caption: All 97 firms; exact released contact-gap pair probabilities and supplied central 90% intervals. The data describe KRW’s historical experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.

apps.name: krw-two
apps.title: Race and gender: one common grade
apps.idea: At the default loss, a common grade beats withholding every pair while each fixed KRW card does so only when its own gap receives enough weight.
apps.from: v2 refill · v2 krw-two rebuilt from v1 storyboard S-03
apps.credit: After Kline, Rose and Walters (2024); archived common report at original settings from postrank 1.1.0 (case_krw_signed97, optimal within solver tolerances); live searches are within the recomputed weighted expected-rank order.
apps.caption: 97 firms of Kline, Rose and Walters (2024). Default live search: τ = .25, at most 4 grades. The data describe KRW's experiment, not any firm's current conduct.

apps.name: cde-cuts
apps.title: Twelve schools: tiers and grades
apps.idea: Dragging two cuts through the twelve schools' posterior order shows that at τ .20 the tertiles state three more pairs than the best report with at most three grades but expect far more wrong directions.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 S-01 case-cde, the cuts view and the comparison panel
apps.credit: 12-school teaching subset as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde).
apps.caption: Twelve-school CDE teaching subset; supplied posterior conditional on a statewide fitted prior. Grade 1 states lowest chronic absence; a shared grade withholds directions.

apps.name: cde-one-disclosure
apps.title: At one disclosure the tertiles win
apps.idea: Of the 34,650 three-grade reports that state 48 pairs, the most three grades allow for twelve schools, the tertiles expect the fewest wrong directions.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 S-01 case-cde, the same-disclosure view
apps.credit: 12-school teaching subset as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde).
apps.caption: Twelve-school CDE teaching subset; supplied posterior conditional on a statewide fitted prior. Grade 1 states lowest chronic absence; a shared grade withholds directions.

apps.name: cde-pair
apps.title: A sure pair left unsaid
apps.idea: At τ = .20, the best report with at most three grades leaves the near-certain F–I direction unsaid. The cheapest report stating it in the same family has slightly higher risk; the four-grade comparison within the posterior-mean order also states it.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 S-01 case-cde, the pair view
apps.credit: 12-school teaching subset as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde).
apps.caption: Twelve-school CDE teaching subset; supplied posterior conditional on a statewide fitted prior. Grade 1 states lowest chronic absence; a shared grade withholds directions.

apps.name: cde-tau-path
apps.title: What each step of τ changes
apps.idea: At each step of τ the schools' best report states more pairs in all, but a step moves a whole block: it can state pairs whose errors exceed the new price and withhold pairs it stated before.
apps.from: v1 view · v1 S-01 case-cde, the τ-path view; adds the pairs each step states and withholds (relationChange)
apps.credit: 12-school teaching subset as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde).
apps.caption: Twelve-school CDE teaching subset; supplied posterior conditional on a statewide fitted prior. Grade 1 states lowest chronic absence; a shared grade withholds directions.

apps.name: alabama-map
apps.title: Alabama counties on two outcomes
apps.idea: On the map one common grade serves both outcomes, yet each outcome keeps its own share of stated directions expected wrong, and the two shares can differ several-fold.
apps.from: v2 refill · v2 alabama rebuilt from v1 storyboard S-04; adds the panel of what each outcome gives up (the archived commonality table at most five grades and τ .20, with status and gap)
apps.credit: Opportunity Atlas data as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_alabama).
apps.caption: 67 Alabama counties (Opportunity Atlas). Default live search: τ = .20, at most 5 grades. Historical outcomes, not current conditions, effects of places or need.

apps.name: your-data
apps.title: Your own posterior summaries
apps.idea: Paste posterior means and SDs (or estimates, SEs and a stated prior), read as independent normal posteriors, and get pair probabilities, a grade report labeled with the family it is best in, and its card.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboard X-01; postrank vignettes a5 and quickstart; picture: messages for each failed check, an independence note, the card, relation matrix and profile with the label of the family used, and R code for the same analysis
apps.credit: Built for this site; your data stay in your browser.
apps.caption: Public examples use declared teaching models. Pasted inputs stay in this component’s memory; the URL carries only public choices and settings. Local exports include the applied inputs and settings.

apps.name: report-designer
apps.title: Grade a case and report it
apps.idea: Choose a case and settings, and get the card with what the report states and leaves unsaid, from the engine's results.
apps.from: new concept · v1 storyboards S-05 and P-14; postrank vignette a6; picture: a case's report card with its family label, budget rows as a feasibility check, relation changes against the archived report, and a sentence of what the report states and leaves unsaid
